clue.text: Age of Information speech starting late, after English ...

indicators.note: a start that comes late begins further in, so the word gives up the letter it opens with

blocks.note: gen is the word for the information you need — 'give me the gen on him'
E is the standard abbreviation for English
a speech is an oration, and one starting late has lost its opening O

explanation.walkthrough: The dots run the sentence on into 6 across, which is what makes 'Age of Information' look like a set phrase when the definition stops at its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Age names a stretch of history defined by the people living through it, which is the same span a generation covers.

clue.text: Heat possibly rising before Spain match

indicators.note: what rises in a down entry climbs towards the top, so those letters are read the other way up

blocks.note: Heat is a celebrity weekly, so it is possibly a mag — and it climbs the entry
E is the international vehicle code for Spain, from Espana

explanation.walkthrough: The capital H is the giveaway that is meant to be missed: this Heat is a title on the newsagent's shelf, not a temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: match -> GAME: a fixture between two sides is called either word, so they swap straight over in football or in tennis.

clue.text: Show outside broadcast in Northern Ireland's capital

indicators.note: putting a thing in somewhere puts it inside, so these letters sit within the ones named next

blocks.note: NI is the everyday abbreviation for Northern Ireland, and it splits to take the rest
to air a programme is to show it
OB is the broadcaster's shorthand for an outside broadcast

explanation.walkthrough: Northern Ireland's capital is Belfast, and the clue is counting on you reaching for it — the two words are letters to be split open, not a country to look up.
explanation.definitionFit: capital -> NAIROBI: Kenya's seat of government, so one particular city is being clued by the general word for what it is.

clue.text: Argyle periodically showing spirit

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at fixed intervals, so you take every second letter and skip the ones between

blocks.note: aRgYlE hands over its second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.walkthrough: Argyle is a sock pattern and Plymouth's football club, and both are decoys: the word is here only to be counted through.
explanation.definitionFit: spirit -> RYE: a whiskey distilled from rye grain, named after the grain, so 'spirit' is the class of drink it belongs to.

clue.text: Dump student taken in by a society's regular drinkers

indicators.note: anything taken in has been swallowed up, so the letter disappears inside the piece that follows

blocks.note: the tip is where you dump the rubbish
per means a — twice per day is twice a day — and it opens up to take the next letter
L-plates mark a learner, the crossword's standing student
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.walkthrough: 'A' for PER is the piece worth banking — pounds a head, miles an hour — and it does the hiding here, because nobody suspects an article.
explanation.definitionFit: regular drinkers -> TIPPLERS: to tipple is to drink habitually rather than heavily, so the word names the routine and not the quantity.

clue.text: Stared at Adele, upset and exposed after pitch error

indicators.note: something upset has been tipped over, and letters tipped over come out in the opposite order
what is exposed has had its covering taken off, so the letters at either end go and the middle is left bare

blocks.note: an own goal, marked OG on the scoresheet, is the error you can only make on a pitch
strip the singer's outer A and E and DEL stands exposed, then tips over

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is doing the misdirection: it sets Adele up as the person being stared at, when the clue wants only the middle of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stared at -> OGLED: to ogle is to stare with open desire, so the definition is the plain act and the answer supplies the leer.

clue.text: ... act's song on piano

indicators.note: in an across entry a piece resting on another is written after it, not above it

blocks.note: p is the mark in a score for piano, meaning softly
a lay is an old word for a song or ballad

explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots carry over from 1 across; ignore them and what is left is a two-piece build with the definition sitting first.
explanation.definitionFit: act -> PLAY: both are verbs for taking a part on stage, so 'act Hamlet' and 'play Hamlet' are the same instruction.

clue.text: Hangs around Liberal, going off Tories

indicators.note: milk that is going off has turned, and letters that have turned no longer sit in the order printed

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal on a ballot paper
the six letters of the party name are the material to be shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: A political surface is the setter's favourite cover for an anagram: 'going off Tories' reads as disillusionment and means only 'rearrange'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangs around -> LOITERS: loitering is lingering with no errand to be on, which is what hanging around a street corner amounts to.

clue.text: Attractive model's daughter becoming Yale's principal

indicators.note: one thing becoming another takes its place, so the letter named first is swapped out for the letter named second
the principal is the one at the head, so only the leading letter of the name beside it is wanted

blocks.note: a tailor's dummy is the model that clothes are fitted on
D is the family-tree abbreviation for daughter, and it is the letter that leaves
the front letter of Yale steps into the vacancy

explanation.walkthrough: A substitution clue always names both letters, the one leaving and the one arriving, so 'becoming' promises a word you know already with one letter changed.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive -> YUMMY: the informal sense that jumps from food to people, where someone yummy is good enough to eat.

clue.text: One of fifty children I amused somewhat when falling over

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the thing, so a run of letters inside these words is all that is wanted
whatever falls over ends up the wrong way up, so the run is read from its far end back

blocks.note: childrEN I AMused holds five letters in an unbroken run, waiting to be read the other way

explanation.walkthrough: Fifty is the American state count, and that is the whole of the definition — everything after it is a hiding place spread across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: One of fifty -> MAINE: the states of the USA number fifty, so giving the total defines any single one of them by example.

clue.text: Cloud facing union's leader amid unruly element

indicators.note: the piece that faces the rest stands at the front of it, with nothing ahead
a leader goes at the head of what follows, so only the first letter of that word is taken
an unruly crowd will not stay in the order it was put in, and nor will these letters

blocks.note: a pall of smoke is a cloud hanging over something
the letter at the head of union
amid reads as a position and is really four letters of material

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'amid', which every solver first reads as an instruction about where something goes. Palladium is element 46, mined mostly for catalytic converters.
explanation.definitionFit: element -> PALLADIUM: a metal with its own square in the periodic table, so the general word for such a substance defines it.

clue.text: Instruction from Madonna, losing head badly when covering metal?

indicators.note: a word that loses its head loses the letter standing at the very front of it
anything done badly comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong come out in the wrong order
a cover goes over the top of what it hides, so this piece wraps round the letters named next

blocks.note: take the M off the front and ADONNA is the letter stock to shuffle
tin is the crossword's handiest metal, and it is wrapped up inside

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark apologises for 'metal': tin is a metal by example, not a definition of one. Andantino is a shade quicker than andante.
explanation.definitionFit: Instruction -> ANDANTINO: the tempo words in a score are instructions to the player, and this one asks for a gently walking pace.

clue.text: Easy listening music? Promote short piece

indicators.note: cut a word short and it comes up one letter shy at the end

blocks.note: MOR is the radio trade's label for middle-of-the-road, the easy listening slot
to promote a product is to sell it, and SELL cut short is SEL

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the tell that easy listening music is being named by its trade abbreviation rather than defined.
explanation.definitionFit: piece -> MORSEL: a morsel is a piece small enough to eat in one go, so the definition is the plain word for the answer's tiny scale.

clue.text: Small uniform, clothing that hurts rear of admiral in vessel

indicators.note: the rear is the back end, so only the final letter of the word behind it is used

blocks.note: S is the clothing-label abbreviation for small
U is uniform in the phonetic alphabet
garb is what a person is clothed in
ow is the noise that means exactly that
the letter at the back of admiral

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothing' looks like an instruction to wrap one piece round another and is really a plain noun — that is the whole trick in a five-piece build.
explanation.definitionFit: vessel -> SUGAR BOWL: vessel is the general word for anything that holds something, and the bowl on the tea tray qualifies.

clue.text: Faltering comedian ending on unintelligible line

indicators.note: the ending on a word is its final letter, and that letter is all this takes from what follows

blocks.note: Ken Dodd, the Liverpool comedian with the tickling stick
the printed word unintelligible, closing letter only
RY is the map abbreviation for a railway line

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ending on unintelligible' asks for a letter of the word as printed, not a synonym for it — a device that reads as ordinary English until you need it.
explanation.definitionFit: Faltering -> DODDERY: doddery describes the unsteady walk of great age, so the faltering is in the legs rather than in the speech.

clue.text: People who shy girls sent almost mad

indicators.note: almost there is not quite there, so the word stops one letter before its end
a mad scramble has no order to it, and letters called mad will not stay where they were put

blocks.note: the five letters of girls go into the pot whole
sent, taken almost to its end, joins them one letter short as SEN

explanation.walkthrough: The awkward part is the reach: 'almost' picks off 'sent' alone and leaves 'girls' untouched, which is why the letter count only works one way.
explanation.definitionFit: People who shy -> SLINGERS: to shy something is to fling it, as at a coconut shy, so the people doing the flinging are slingers.

clue.text: Relative clears Chianti bottles last of all

indicators.note: last of all points at the very end of every word in turn, and nothing before it counts

blocks.note: the closing letters of clearS chiantI bottleS

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a container instruction, and a wine word in a wine surface is exactly where you would expect one — it is really the third word being trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Relative -> SIS: the clipped, affectionate form of sister, so the answer is a family member named by the household shorthand.

clue.text: Idle American bores classy new journalist

indicators.note: to bore is to drill straight into something, and what bores into a word finishes up inside it

blocks.note: U is the label from U and non-U speech, the crossword's word for classy
N is the standard abbreviation for new
ed, short for editor, is the crossword journalist, and the drilling happens just before it
US is the American doing the boring

explanation.walkthrough: U for classy comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U speech, and it is the setter's standing shorthand for anything posh.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle -> UNUSED: machinery standing idle is machinery nobody is using, so the word describes disuse rather than laziness.

clue.text: Robin perhaps lifted by hand now and then

indicators.note: a piece lifted up a down entry is carried back towards the top, so it is read upwards
now and then means every so often rather than throughout, so occasional letters are taken and the rest left

blocks.note: bY hAnD gives up its second, fourth and sixth letters, which then climb the entry

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Robin Day was the BBC's great political interviewer, and 'perhaps' is the flag that a surname is being clued through one of the people who bore it.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin perhaps -> DAY: a definition by example, the broadcaster Robin Day, so the first name is pointing at the surname beside it.

clue.text: Move seats and get props and scenery

indicators.note: moving a thing takes it out of the place it was in, and letters moved will not stay in their printed order

blocks.note: the eight letters of the two words, with 'and' just holding them together

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as instructions to the stage crew, which is the joke: 'move seats and get' is the material rather than the job.
explanation.definitionFit: props and scenery -> STAGE SET: the set is everything dressing a stage for a scene, which is the props and the scenery taken together.

clue.text: "Give us a twirl!" Games with King Brucie at the front, terrific

indicators.note: give something a twirl and it spins round to face the other way
the front of a name is where its first letter stands, and that letter is all this asks for

blocks.note: the setter's own 'us', two letters ready to be spun
PE, physical education, is games on the school timetable
R is Rex, the Latin king
the front letter of Bruce Forsyth's nickname

explanation.walkthrough: Bruce Forsyth's catchphrase is a whole quoted sentence doing one small job, turning two letters round, and then Brucie turns up again as an initial.
explanation.definitionFit: terrific -> SUPERB: both sit at the top of the scale of praise, terrific having drifted from causing terror to plain excellence.

clue.text: Under pressure formerly, are United level?

indicators.note: in a down entry whatever is under something hangs below it, so the thing named first is passed before the rest

blocks.note: P is the physicist's abbreviation for pressure
the late king is the former one, so late does duty for formerly
an are is a metric unit of area, written a, and a hundred of them make a hectare
U is how United is written on a league table

explanation.walkthrough: A crossword 'are' is almost always the unit of area rather than the verb, and it is worth banking, because the verb is what the eye sees every time.
explanation.definitionFit: level -> PLATEAU: high ground that has stopped rising, so as a noun the answer names the flat stretch across the top.

clue.text: Case for Turandot lyrics being translated to the letter?

indicators.note: a case encloses what is inside it, so the case for a word is the pair of letters at its two ends
a translation says the same thing in wholly different characters, which is what happens to these

blocks.note: the opera's name keeps only its two end letters, one T at each
the six letters of lyrics join them in the pot

explanation.walkthrough: Turandot is italicised because it is a title, and those italics are the only hint that the word is being handled as letters rather than as an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: to the letter -> STRICTLY: obeying an instruction to the letter is obeying it strictly, exactly as written and with no latitude allowed.

clue.text: Primate thanks sailor without hesitation

indicators.note: here it means lacking rather than outside, so the letters named next are taken away

blocks.note: ta is the informal thanks
a mariner is a sailor
er is the noise of hesitation, and it is the pair of letters that comes out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' points at monkeys here rather than archbishops — the other sense the word carries, and the one the churchy surface would rather you tried.
explanation.definitionFit: Primate -> TAMARIN: a small South American monkey, so one species is standing in under the name of the whole order.

clue.text: Charm of hair swept back over curl in the centre

indicators.note: hair swept back goes the other way, and so do the letters of the word for it
what sits in the centre is neither end, so the outer letters are left behind

blocks.note: a mane is a head of hair, here written from the back
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
the middle two letters of cURl

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all hairdressing and every word of it does a different job: one word to reverse, one cricket abbreviation, one word to take the middle out of.
explanation.definitionFit: Charm -> ENAMOUR: to enamour someone is to make them fall for you, which is charm working on the heart rather than on the manners.

clue.text: Like judge probing opera company? Initially, yes

indicators.note: a probe goes into whatever it examines, so this letter is pushed inside the piece named next
initially means at the outset, so only the opening letter of the word it points at is used

blocks.note: ENO is English National Opera, and the probe goes in after its first two letters
J is how a judge is abbreviated in a law report, as in Smith J
the opening letter of yes

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that 'opera company' means one particular company rather than the general idea, and ENO is the set of initials you are expected to know.
explanation.definitionFit: Like -> ENJOY: the sense in 'I like a good thriller' — taking pleasure in the thing rather than being fond of a person.

clue.text: Just female getting away from the creeps, ...

indicators.note: whatever gets away from a word is no longer in it, so that letter is subtracted

blocks.note: giving somebody the creeps is giving them a fright
F is the standard abbreviation for female, and it is the letter that escapes

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the sentence on into 26 down, so the comma and dots at the end are punctuation rather than anything to parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Just -> RIGHT: the sense of fair and deserved, as in a just cause being a right one, not right as correct or as a direction.

clue.text: German ladies say brother's dim

indicators.note: say marks an example rather than a synonym: the word before it is one particular instance of what is wanted

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
the Ladies is one of the two doors on a pub loo
brother! and my! are the same mild exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: Two exclamations meeting is the joke — 'brother!' and 'my!' are both what people say when something is mildly too much.
explanation.definitionFit: dim -> GLOOMY: both describe light that has gone poor, and gloomy adds the mood that the dimness puts you in.

clue.text: ... vacuous admirers, posers and snakes

indicators.note: a vacuous thing is empty in the middle, so each word beside it keeps only the letters at its two ends

blocks.note: hollow out admirers and its first and last letters are what remain
posers emptied the same way leaves its outer pair

explanation.walkthrough: One 'vacuous' serves both words at once, which is why the comma is carrying more weight than it looks: it holds two identical operations together.
explanation.definitionFit: snakes -> ASPS: the asp is the small Egyptian viper of the Cleopatra story, so one kind of snake stands under the general word.

clue.text: Book records for auditor, average kind of chap

indicators.note: an auditor is somebody who listens, so what counts is how the words sound and not how they are spelt

blocks.note: Job is the Old Testament book of suffering and patience
a ship's logs are its records
run the two together and say them aloud: the B slides across the gap between the words

explanation.walkthrough: A biblical book and a shelf of logs are two flat nouns until you say them quickly, and what falls out is the name we give to nobody in particular.
explanation.definitionFit: average kind of chap -> JOE BLOGGS: the British name of choice for the man in the street, where an American would say John Doe.

clue.text: Republican interrupting scoundrel's brag?

definitions.note: Brag is one particular game while the answer is plural: the pastime played with a pack has no singular in English, so a single game has to stand for all of them.

indicators.note: an interruption arrives in the middle of something already under way, so this letter lands inside the other word

blocks.note: a cad is the crossword's scoundrel, and the 's supplies the closing letter
R is the abbreviation for Republican in American election coverage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brag' reads as boasting right up to the question mark, which is the only signal that the word is a noun and the name of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: brag -> CARDS: brag is a three-card gambling game, ancestor of poker, so naming it with a question mark points at the pack it is played with.

clue.text: Being cut off from papa affected banker

indicators.note: cutting one thing off from another removes it, so the letter named goes out of the word beside it

blocks.note: affected manners are camp
papa is P in the phonetic alphabet, and P is the letter cut off here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is the crossword's favourite lie: not somebody who works in a bank but a thing that has banks, which is to say a river.
explanation.definitionFit: banker -> CAM: the Cam is the river running through Cambridge, and a river earns the name banker by being the thing with banks.

clue.text: Solver's Yankee ball game in retirement

indicators.note: something in retirement has withdrawn from where it stood, so these letters go back the way they came

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the phonetic alphabet
a ball drawn on paper is a plain round O
RU is rugby union, and it is the piece that withdraws

explanation.walkthrough: Only the game turns round, not the ball: 'in retirement' reaches back a single word, and testing how far an indicator reaches is half of solving one.
explanation.definitionFit: Solver's -> YOUR: the setter is addressing whoever holds the pencil, so anything belonging to the solver is yours.

clue.text: Maybe 9 soldiers tense before special bulletins

indicators.note: what comes before something is written ahead of it, so of these two letters that one goes first

blocks.note: 9 across turns out to be MAINE, which is maybe a state
soldiers are the men in the ranks
T is the grammarian's abbreviation for tense
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.walkthrough: A bare number is a cross-reference, so 9 across has to be solved first, and 'maybe' is then the flag that the answer there is one example of a wider word.
explanation.definitionFit: bulletins -> STATEMENTS: an official statement issued to the press is a bulletin, so the two are the same announcement under different names.
